# Introduction
This report sets out to critically review and attempt to replicate the analysis by @arif_2022. 

# Review

## Causal question and predictor variables
The main causal question in this paper is well defined as: how did specific key variables each causally affect the recovery trajectories of coral reefs in the Seychelles following bleaching events in 1998? [@graham_2015]. This main causal question is outlined in the abstract and revisited throughout the text. Causal inference is the prediction of intervention [@pearl_2009], and here the causal question is predicting whether changes in any of the key variables would change the recovery trajectory of a reef. Rather than a single causal question, this analysis is essentially a series of causal questions aimed at determining the effects on a single response variable. The question is fairly specific indicating that the results apply only to these reefs in the Seychelles and this specific bleaching event. The authors recognise the limitations of the causal relationships by not attempting to generalise to other coral reef localities. Although, the defined causal model, was used to predict the recovery trajectory following a bleaching event in 2016 for the same original reefs which had since recovered from the 1998 bleaching event. 

Some details about the predictor variables were omitted from the paper but these were mostly available in the earlier research by @graham_2015. The alternative recovery trajectories of coral reefs were defined as a binary variable of recovering or regime shifting as per @graham_2015. Recovering reefs had coral cover greater than macroalgal coverage and time series data showed high or increasing coral cover while regime shifting reefs showed macroalgae dominance greater than coral cover and macroalgal cover remained high or increased over time [@graham_2015]. Four metrics were used to define recovery trajectories with the full methodology described in @graham_2015. Data collection for the branching coral cover, macroalgal cover, herbivorous fish biomass, and structural complexity variables was stated as 1994 and could thus be considered as pre-bleaching conditions. Collection dates for the other variables prior were not stated but could be found in the literature [@graham_2015]. There was however a discrepancy relating the the data collection for the nutrient measurements. @arif_2022 stated that these data were from 2004 and suggested @graham_2015 as the source of the data but according to @graham_2015 nutrient measurements were collected in 2014. This may have been a typographical error. The 2014 data from @graham_2015 is unfortunately unavailable thus it cannot be cross-checked. If this is not a typographical error, the source of the nutrient data should have been cited or data collection described. Either way, the nutrient measurements were taken after the bleaching event occurred. Nutrient content is expected to change over seasons but differences in sites are anticipated to remain stable [@graham_2015]. Nevertheless, there is the possibility for the post-bleaching macroalgal content to affect nutrient levels which would be an issue for causal inference from measurements taken post-bleaching. Depth, MPA, and wave exposure data were expected to remain stable over time thus even though depth was measured and wave exposure was calculated post-bleaching (1998 - 2011), this should not be an issue for inference as macroalgae content post-bleaching should not affect depth, MPA, or wave exposure. 

##  Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) specification
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) are a commonly utilised tool for specifying causal models. The specification of the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) for the causal question here was appropriate as it used domain knowledge and extensive research on the issue of coral bleaching. There was a detailed explanation in the supplementary text for each of the causal relationship included in the DAG. I inspected the stated relationships and they were all justifiable. There were no potentially unobserved variables included in the DAG. This may be because no other variables were recognised to be related to any of the variables in the current DAG. Alternatively, there is a risk that that the DAG was created around the variables for which data were available, especially since this analysis was done retrospectively on data previously collected for a "causal salad" model of coral reef bleaching. The omission of variables may have negative effects ... [talk about colliders etc]

There was discrepancy between the DAG downloaded from dagitty.net in the supplied code and the DAG stated in the paper [@arif_2022]. The downloaded DAG contained a directed edge from depth to initial macroalgae cover and excluded the directed edge from wave exposure to branching coral unlike the DAG in the paper. The causal relationships described and the d-separation conditions examined in the supplementary information were associated with the DAG in the paper. After checks it was found that the data were in fact consistent with the d-separation conditions implied by both DAGs. The d-separation method is a way to test for DAG-data consistency [@pearl_2009]. In addition to a DAG being defensible based on ecological theory, all d-separation conditions or independencies implied by a given DAG should be consistent with the data in order for the DAG to be utilised. These inconsistencies in DAG structure does raise the question of whether the final causal model stated in the paper was the first to be proposed or whether alternative DAGs, such as the one in the supplied code, were tested. The authors recognise that multiple DAGs can pass DAG-data consistency, and that the final DAG should be justified with theory but do not outline their consideration of alternative DAGs. Ideally, an analysis of alternative DAGs and explanation of why the final causal model was chosen should have been included, especially since the data were consistent with both of these DAGs yet DAG choice may affect the causal models specifications and thus results. 

### The causal adjustment strategy
The authors used the backdoor criterion to define an adjustment set for each variable in order to estimate the total causal effect of the given variable on the recovery trajectory of coral reefs. This is an established method for calculating sets of variables to adjust for to give an unbiased estimate of the total causal effect of one variable on another [@pearl_2009]. All the models specified in the paper satisfy the backdoor criterion for the DAG used in the paper. The model specifications for some of the variables would change if the DAG in the supplied code were used instead (such as branching coral). For the majority of variables including MPA, depth, wave exposure, nutrients, branching, structural complexity, and herbivore biomass, the minimal adjustment set was used for the model specifications, meaning the set containing the fewest variables which satisfies the backdoor criterion. However, for the initial macroalgae model, depth was included as a covariate even though the minimal adjustment set does not include this variable. The adjustment set still satisfies the backdoor criterion with depth included, it is just not the minimal adjustment set. The inclusion of depth might be as a result of the use of the DAG in the supplied code prior to the final DAG included in the paper. The supplementary text hints at this with the inclusion of paths 5 and 6 which do not exist in the DAG in the paper but do exist in the DAG in the supplied code. The directed edge from depth to initial macroalgae opens additional backdoor paths which should be adjusted for by including depth when using the DAG in the supplied code. Reasons for the decision to use the minimal adjustment sets for the other variables and not to use the minimal adjustment set for the initial macroalgae model should have been explicitly stated. While all adjustment sets which satisfy the backdoor criterion give unbiased estimates of the total causal effect but they can differ in precision of the estimates depending on the additional variables included [@pearl_2009]. 

There were additional errors in the supplementary information for this section (S1.3). The initial macroalgae model had an incomplete path (path 4) listed, although this did not affect the adjustment set. The model specified in the paper for herbivore biomass which adjusts for structural complexity and MPA is the minimial set satisfying the backdoor criterion. However, the supplementary text description has an error stating that structural complexity and branching coral should be adjusted for. This is incorrect as this is insufficient as an adjustment set since branching coral is a collider and opens another backdoor path (Herbivore biomass <- MPA -> Branching coral <- Depth -> Regime Shift) thus MPA or Depth would still additionally need to be included in the set to block this newly opened path.

# Reproduction
In order to reproduce the analysis by @arif_2022, I obtained the data and R code supplied from Figshare [@arif_2021] and modified the code in R [@R]. (As alluded to above, the metadata for the supplied data was poor with no description for any of the four datasets nor the variables within them other than what could be drawn from the paper, the supplementary data, and the code.) I read in the four datasets and checked for missing values. Checked that the standardised data were correctly standardised 

## Causal analysis
I did not reproduce the creation of the DAG as this requires extensive knowledge about coral reef systems. Additionally, the reasons for the directed relationships within the DAG are well outlined in the supplementary text. After reading in the DAG from dagitty.web using the *dagitty* package [@dagitty], I noted that the DAG in the code differed from that in the paper as previously mentioned. Thus, I modified the DAG layout code to reflect the DAG in the paper (Figure \@ref(fig:DAG-fig)). I confirmed that there were 32 DAG-implied independencies, cross-checked them against those listed in the supplementary data, and confirmed that the observed data were consistent with the independencies (p = 1) after performing Holm-Bonferroni correction to p-values to account for multiple testing. To assess the selection of covariates in the models for each variable, I manually drew the DAG and used the backdoor criterion to determine which variables to adjust for. I also made use of the adjustmentSets function from *dagitty* to determine the minimal adjustment set for each of the variables [@dagitty]. As noted above, the minimal adjustment set was used for all variables except the initial macroalgae model in the paper. For the remainder of the analysis, I made use of the models stated in the paper since these all still satisfied the backdoor criterion.

# Standardised data - this was used in analysis
SeychellesS <- read_xlsx("data/SeychellesS.xlsx") %>%

         across(c(MPA, Depth, Branching, Struccomplex, Nutrients, Herb, Macro...16), as.numeric))

summary(SeychellesS)
any(is.na(SeychellesS))

# Unstandardised data
Seychelles <- read_xlsx("data/Seychelles.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(Wave = as.numeric(Wave)) # change from character
str(Seychelles)
summary(Seychelles)
any(is.na(Seychelles))

# Check that SeychellesS is in fact the correct standardised data
Seychelles %>% mutate(
  across(c(Manage, Depth, Branching, Struccomplex, Nutrients, Wave, Macro, Herb), 
  ~(.x - mean(.x)) / (2*sd(.x))))

# 2014 observational dataset for prediction

  mutate(Wave = as.numeric(Wave)) # change from character
Predictions <- read_xlsx("data/Predictions.xlsx")

```{r DAG}
# Test DAG-data consistency

# Download DAG from dagitty.net
DAG <- downloadGraph("dagitty.net/mbt1AvL") 

# Visualise DAG
plot(graphLayout(DAG))

# View conditional independencies
print(impliedConditionalIndependencies(DAG))
length(impliedConditionalIndependencies(DAG))

# Evaluate the d-separation implications of the DAG
r <- localTests(x = DAG, data = SeychellesS %>% 
                  select(MPA, Branching, Struccomplex, Herb, Shifted, Depth, Nutrients, Macro...16, Wave) %>%
                  rename(Nutrient = Nutrients, Macro = Macro...16))
r

# Perform Holm-Bonferroni correction to p-values
r$p.value <- p.adjust(r$p.value)
r
# p-values all 1 indicate DAG-data consistency 

# View minimal adjustment sets when using the backdoor criterion (i.e. effect = "total")
adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "MPA", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total") 
adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "Nutrient", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total") 
adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "Herb", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total")

adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "Macro", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total") 
adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "Macro", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total") 
adjustmentSets(DAG, exposure = "Macro", outcome = "Shifted", effect = "total")

cat(as.character(DAG))

As in the analysis by @arif_2022, I used the *rethinking* package [@rethinking] to fit Bayesian logistic regression models for each of the variables of interest with the response being 0 for recovering sites and 1 for regime shifting sites. The data for the 1998 bleaching event were standardised by subtracting the mean of each variable and dividing by two standard deviations prior to model fitting. I used the supplied standardised dataset but checked that this corresponded with  standardisation applied to the original dataset. Weakly informative priors were used including a Cauchy(0,10) prior for the intercept terms and student_t(4,0,2.5) priors for slope coefficients as recommended by previous authors and utilised in the paper. I used three chains rather than a single chain as in @arif_2022 to assess convergence. I also made use of the more recently introduced ulam tool rather than map2stan for model fitting [@rethinking]. All chains converged with Rhat < 1.01 for all parameters and traceplots showed appropriate mixing.

I plotted the posterior median with 90% and 50% percentile intervals (PI) for the causal effect of each of the variables on regime shift trajectory on the logit scale (log-odds). The paper stated that the solid lines in the plot represented the 95% highest posterior density intervals (HPDI). However, the code and the actual plot indicate that PIs not HPDIs were calculated so this is what was replicated (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-3)a). It may have been better to plot effect sizes using the odd ratios on a log scale as these are more easily interpreted. Marginal plots of the continuous predictor variables were also plotted by refitting the causal Bayesian logistic regression models for each variable with the stan_glm function and computing the marginal means and 95% predictive intervals for the given predictor with ggpredict (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-3)(b-h)). These figures were all reproducible exactly as Figure 3 in @arif_2022.

```{r bayesian_models}
# Use ulam with cmdstan rather than map2stan

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Shifted ~ bernoulli(p)

#--------------------------------
## MPA model: 
# logit(p) = beta0 + beta1 * MPA

MPA_mod <- ulam(
  flist = # flist contains the formulas that define the likelihood and priors
    alist(Shifted ~ dbinom(1, p), # shifted has bernoulli distribution
          logit(p) <- beta0 + beta1 * MPA, # logistic model
          beta0 ~ dcauchy(0, 10), # priors on beta0
          beta1 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5) # priors on beta1
    ), 
  data = SeychellesS %>% select(Shifted, MPA), 
  chains = 3,
  cmdstan = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE, 
  refresh = 0,
  show_messages = FALSE)

precis(MPA_mod) # summary statistics for posteriors
plot(MPA_mod) # visual representations of summary statistics
rethinking::traceplot(MPA_mod) # traceplots

# show median and 90% and 50% percentile interval (PI) for depth  
post <- extract.samples(MPA_mod)
post_MPA <- post$beta1
PI90_MPA <- PI(post_MPA, prob = 0.90)
PI50_MPA <- PI(post_MPA, prob = 0.50) 
HPDI_MPA <- HPDI(post_MPA, prob = 0.95) 
med_MPA <- median(post_MPA) 
str(SeychellesS)

#--------------------------------
## Nutrient model: 
# logit(p) = beta0 + beta1 * Nutrients + beta2 * Depth

nutrient_mod <- ulam(
  flist = 
    alist(Shifted ~ dbinom(1, p),
          logit(p) <- beta0 + beta1 * Nutrients + beta2 * Depth,
          beta0 ~ dcauchy(0, 10),
          beta1 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta2 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5)
    ), 
  data = SeychellesS %>% select(Shifted, Nutrients, Depth), 
  chains = 3,
  cmdstan = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE, 
  refresh = 0,
  show_messages = FALSE)

precis(nutrient_mod) # summary statistics for posteriors
plot(nutrient_mod) # visual representations of summary statistics
rethinking::traceplot(nutrient_mod) # traceplots

# show median and 90% and 50% percentile interval (PI) for depth  
post <- extract.samples(nutrient_mod)
post_nutrient <- post$beta1
PI90_nutrient <- PI(post_nutrient, prob = 0.90)
PI50_nutrient <- PI(post_nutrient, prob = 0.50) 
HPDI_nutrient <- HPDI(post_nutrient, prob = 0.95) 
med_nutrient <- median(post_nutrient) 

#--------------------------------
## Herbivore biomass model:
# logit(p) = beta0 + beta1 * Herb + beta2 * MPA + beta3 * Struccomplex

herb_mod <- ulam(
  flist = 
    alist(Shifted ~ dbinom(1, p),
          logit(p) <- beta0 + beta1 * Herb + beta2 * MPA + beta3 * Struccomplex ,
          beta0 ~ dcauchy(0, 10),
          beta1 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta2 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta3 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5)
    ), 
  data = SeychellesS %>% select(Shifted, Herb, MPA, Struccomplex), 
  chains = 3,
  cmdstan = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE, 
  refresh = 0,
  show_messages = FALSE)

precis(herb_mod) # summary statistics for posteriors
plot(herb_mod) # visual representations of summary statistics
rethinking::traceplot(herb_mod) # traceplots

# show median and 90% and 50% percentile interval (PI) for depth  
post <- extract.samples(herb_mod)
post_herb <- post$beta1
PI90_herb <- PI(post_herb, prob = 0.90)
PI50_herb <- PI(post_herb, prob = 0.50) 
HPDI_herb <- HPDI(post_herb, prob = 0.95) 
med_herb <- median(post_herb) 


#--------------------------------
## Branching coral model:
# logit(p) = beta0 + beta1 * Branching + beta2 * MPA + beta3 * Depth + beta4 * Wave

branching_mod <- ulam(
  flist = 
    alist(Shifted ~ dbinom(1, p),
          logit(p) <- beta0 + beta1 * Branching + beta2 * MPA + beta3 * Depth + beta4 * Wave,
          beta0 ~ dcauchy(0, 10),
          beta1 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta2 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta3 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5),
          beta4 ~ dstudent(4, 0, 2.5)
    ), 
  data = SeychellesS %>% select(Shifted, Branching, MPA, Depth, Wave), 
  chains = 3,
  cmdstan = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE, 
  refresh = 0,
  show_messages = FALSE)

precis(branching_mod) # summary statistics for posteriors
plot(branching_mod) # visual representations of summary statistics
rethinking::traceplot(branching_mod) # traceplots

# show median and 90% and 50% percentile interval (PI) for depth

PI50_branching <- PI(post_branching, prob = 0.50)

## Initial macroalgae biomass model:

  flist =

  rename(Macro = Macro...16), 
  chains = 3,
  cmdstan = TRUE,
  messages = FALSE, 
  refresh = 0,
  show_messages = FALSE)

precis(macro_mod) # summary statistics for posteriors
plot(macro_mod) # visual representations of summary statistics
rethinking::traceplot(macro_mod) # traceplots

# show median and 90% and 50% percentile interval (PI) for depth  
post <- extract.samples(macro_mod)
post_macro <- post$beta1
PI90_macro <- PI(post_macro, prob = 0.90)
PI50_macro <- PI(post_macro, prob = 0.50) 
HPDI_macro <- HPDI(post_macro, prob = 0.95) 
med_macro <- median(post_macro) 

```

```{r marginal_causal_plots}
## Plot marginal plots of continuous predictor variables as shown in Figure 3b and 4b. Use ‘Seychelles’ dataset, which has unstandardized data.
# Requires fitting Bayesian glms for each response variable using MCMC

# Define function for plotting
plot_3b <- function(ggpred_obj, x_label, percentage = FALSE, scale_down = FALSE) {
  
  i <- which(diff(ggpred_obj$predicted > 0.5) != 0)[1] # first prediction greater than 0.5
  x_50 <- approx(x = ggpred_obj$predicted[i:(i + 1)], y = ggpred_obj$x[i:(i + 1)], xout = 0.5)$y # interpolation to find approximate coordinate along the line, then extract y coord
  
  p <- plot(ggpred_obj, show_data = TRUE, 
            jitter = 0.0, dot_size = 1, line_size = 0.5, 
            show_title = FALSE, show_y_title = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
    labs(x = x_label) + 
    theme(aspect.ratio = 1) + # 1:1 aspect ratio
    annotate("point", x = x_50, y = 0.5, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "steelblue") # add diamond with calculated value
  
  # If percentage is true, rescale the x axis to % scale
  if (percentage) { 
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1, suffix = ""))
    }
  
  # If percentage is true, rescale the x axis by 10 000 (for herbivore biomass)
  if (scale_down) {
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01, scale = 1/10000))
  }
  p
}

# Depth marginal plot 
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Depth, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1, refresh = 0)
depth_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Depth")
plot_depth <- plot_3b(depth_MP, "Depth (m)")

# Nutrient marginal plot 
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Nutrients + Depth, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1, refresh = 0)
nutrient_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Nutrients")
plot_nutrient <- plot_3b(nutrient_MP, "Carbon : Nitrogen")

# Branching coral marginal plot

branching_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Branching")
plot_branching <- plot_3b(branching_MP, "Branching Coral (% cover)", percentage = TRUE)

# Structural complexity marginal plot

# Wave exposure marginal plot

plot_wave <- plot_3b(wave_MP, "Wave Exposure")

# Herbivore biomass marginal plot

## DAG-informed predictive model
A causally guided predictive model was created in @arif_2022 to determine the potential trajectory of 12 recovering reef sites after subsequent bleaching events in 2016. The predictor variables used by the authors comprised those directly influencing the response based on the DAG including depth, nutrients, branching coral, structural complexity, wave exposure, and initial macroalagal cover. Herbivorous fish biomass was excluded as a predictor since herbivorous fish biomass was not found to be a good proxy for herbivore grazing pressure. A Bayesian logistic regression model with weakly informative priors was used for the predictive model. The model was fitted to the unstandardised dataset from the 1998 bleaching event using the map function from *rethinking* [@rethinking]. Normally distributed priors with mean zero and standard deviation of 10 were used for both the intercept and slope coefficients. I verified that the model correctly predicted the recovery trajectory for 19 out of 21 sites, with incorrect predictions for Cousin Patch and St Anne Granite reefs, using posterior predictive checks and assuming 1000 samples from the posterior and a threshold of 0.5. 

This trained model was used to predict recovery trajectories for the recovering reefs post-1998 bleaching after the 2016 bleaching event using 2014 data. The supplied code predicted on all 21 reefs using the link function with 1000 samples. I restricted the prediction to only the 12 recovering reefs and reproduced Figure 4a [@arif_2022] by plotting the posterior probabilities (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-4)a). I obtained similar results to the paper, with a few small differences in posterior means (for example, St Anne P and G) likely due random selection of the 1000 samples. I set the seed to ensure reproducibility of my analysis. Despite these small differences, these results confirmed that five reefs had a probability greater than 50% of shifting regime to macroalgae dominance based on their posterior means (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-4)a). The marginal plots of the continuous predictor variables were replotted for the continuous variables included in the predictive model. For each variable, I overlaid data points from reefs where the variable's value corresponded to a regime-shift probability greater than 0.5. The ranges over which marginal means were predicted were extended for the structural complexity and macroalgae cover variables so as to include the overlaid data points.

```{r predictive_model}
# Predictive model for predicting which of the 12 recovering reefs are expected to regime shift following the 2016 bleaching event 

# Train model using ‘Seychelles’ dataset 

set.seed(1) # for reproducibility

SeyPre <- map(
  alist(
    Shifted ~ dbinom( 1 , p ) ,
    logit(p) <- a  + bd*Depth + bn*Nutrients + bw*Wave + bic*Struccomplex  + bbc*Branching + bim*Macro,
    a ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bn ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bw ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bic ~ dnorm(0,10),
    bbc ~ dnorm(0,30),
    bim ~ dnorm(0,10)
  ), 
  data = Seychelles)

# Posterior Validation Check
postcheck(SeyPre, n = 1000) # x axis is each of the regions, blue circle is the actual shifted status and clear circle is the predicted value with predictive interval

# 19 out of 21 incorrectly predicted
# 3 and 20 incorrectly predicted

```

```{r posterior_predictive_plots}

# Predict using 2014 observational dataset “Seychelles2014” 
# Only want to predict for recovering reefs
# so extract list of reefs recovering
recovering <- Seychelles2014 %>% filter(Shifted == 0) 
recovering_names <- recovering %>% select(Region) %>% pull()

set.seed(1)
predict <- link(SeyPre, data = recovering) # Computes inverse-link linear model values
str(predict)
summary(predict)
dim(predict)
head(predict)

# Rename columns to correct region 
colnames(predict) <- recovering_names

# Extract means for naming
predict_means <- apply(predict, 2, mean) %>% round(2)

# Rather than reading in and using the dataset “Predictions” which show the individual probabilities of regime shifting estimated for each recovering reef site, reformat the data we have
plot_predictive_effects <- predict %>% data.frame() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), # reformat for plotting
               names_to = "Reef Site", 
               values_to = "Probability of Regime Shift") %>% 
  mutate(`Reef Site` = paste0(`Reef Site`, " (", round(predict_means[`Reef Site`] * 100), 
  "%)")) %>% # add mean posterior predictions
  # Reformat names
  mutate(`Reef Site` = gsub("_", " ", `Reef Site`),
         `Reef Site` = gsub("atch", "", `Reef Site`),
         `Reef Site` = gsub("ranite", "", `Reef Site`),
         `Reef Site` = gsub("arbonate", "", `Reef Site`),
         `Reef Site` = gsub("Ste", "St", `Reef Site`)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = `Probability of Regime Shift`, y = 	`Reef Site`)) + # plot
  geom_density_ridges(aes(fill = `Reef Site`)) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("yellowgreen", "yellow", 	"orange", "red2", "deeppink", "purple", "lightsteelblue3", 	"darkblue", "slateblue4", "blue", "deepskyblue3", 	"cadetblue2")) +
  labs(y = "") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1.5) # 1:1 aspect ratio
  
```

```{r marginal_predictive_plots}

# Create dataframe of colours for each region for plotting
colour_match <- recovering %>% 
  arrange(Region) %>% 
  mutate(Colour = c("yellowgreen", "yellow", 	"orange", "red2", "deeppink", "purple", "lightsteelblue3", 	"darkblue", "slateblue4", "blue", "deepskyblue3", 	"cadetblue2")) %>%
  select(Region, Colour)

# Define function for plotting 4b
plot_4b <- function(ggpred_obj, x_label, percentage = FALSE) {
  
  var_of_interest <- attr(ggpred_obj, "terms") # extract the variable of interest name
  
  # T or F for whether function is increasing or not
  is_increasing <- tail(ggpred_obj$predicted, 1) > head(ggpred_obj$predicted, 1)
  
  # Identify points along the curve where probability > 0.5
  
  # if function is increasing
  if (is_increasing) {
    i <- which(diff(ggpred_obj$predicted > 0.5) != 0)[1] # after which prediction is y > 0.5
    x_50 <- approx(x = ggpred_obj$predicted[i:(i + 1)], y = ggpred_obj$x[i:(i + 1)], xout = 0.5)$y # interpolation to find approximate coordinate along the line, then extract y coord
    x_points <- recovering %>% filter(.data[[var_of_interest]] > x_50) # find which values of branching when y is greater than 0.5 
  } else { # if decreasing, switch > to <
    i <- which(diff(ggpred_obj$predicted < 0.5) != 0)[1] 
    x_50 <- approx(x = ggpred_obj$predicted[i:(i + 1)], y = ggpred_obj$x[i:(i + 1)], xout = 0.5)$y 
    x_points <- recovering %>% filter(.data[[var_of_interest]] < x_50) 
  }

  y_points <- sapply(x_points[[var_of_interest]], function(val) {
    i2 <- which(diff(ggpred_obj$x > val) != 0)[1] # for these x values after which prediction is y > these values
    if (is.na(i2)) return(NA) # if there are no points
    
    # interpolation to find approximate coordinate along the line, then extract y coord
    approx(x = ggpred_obj$x[i2:(i2 + 1)], 
           y = ggpred_obj$predicted[i2:(i2 + 1)], 
           xout = val)$y 
  })
  
  points_to_plot <- data.frame(x = x_points[[var_of_interest]],
                               y = y_points)
  
  p <- plot(ggpred_obj, show_data = TRUE, 
            jitter = 0.0, dot_size = 1, line_size = 0.5, 
            show_title = FALSE, show_y_title = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
    labs(x = x_label) + 
    theme(aspect.ratio = 1) + # 1:1 aspect ratio
    geom_point(data = points_to_plot, aes(x = x, y = y), 
               shape = 19, size = 4, 
               colour = pull(colour_match %>% filter(Region %in% x_points$Region) %>% select(Colour)))

  if (percentage) { 
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1, suffix = ""))
    }
  
  p
  
}

# Depth marginal plot 
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Depth, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1)
depth_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Depth")
plot_depth <- plot_4b(depth_MP, "Depth (m)")

# Nutrient marginal plot  -- check this one again, extra point
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Nutrients + Depth, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1)
nutrient_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Nutrients")
plot_nutrient <- plot_4b(nutrient_MP, "Carbon : Nitrogen")

# Branching coral marginal plot -- check this one again, axis scale
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Branching + Depth + Manage + Wave, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1) 
branching_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Branching")
plot_branching <- plot_4b(branching_MP, "Branching Coral (% cover)", percentage = TRUE)

# Structural complexity marginal plot -- points different order
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Struccomplex + Branching, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"),chains = 1)
struccomplex_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Struccomplex[1.5:4 by=0.1]") 
plot_complexity <- plot_4b(struccomplex_MP, "Structural Complexity")

# Wave exposure marginal plot -- points shifted slightly
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Wave, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1)
wave_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Wave")
plot_wave <- plot_4b(wave_MP, "Wave Exposure")

# Initial macroalgae cover marginal plot -- doesn't add point
fit <- stan_glm(Shifted ~ Macro + Herb + Depth + Nutrients + Wave, data = Seychelles, family = binomial("logit"), chains = 1)
macro_MP <- ggpredict(fit, terms = "Macro[0:20.1 by=0.1]") 
plot_macro <- plot_4b(macro_MP, "Macroalgae (% cover)")
